rules.name: no-process-killer
rules.reason: A pattern-matching process killer takes down anything whose command line happens to match, including this session and unrelated work on the same machine. Find the process first (`ps aux | grep '[m]yserver'`) and kill the PID you actually meant.

rules.name: no-recursive-force-delete
rules.reason: A recursive forced delete has no undo and no confirmation, and the option set is what matters rather than how it was spelled: `-rf`, `-fr`, `-vrf`, `-r -f`, `-R -f` and `--recursive --force` are one command. Name the directory you created (`rm -rf ./build`), and if the flags arrived through a variable, write them out so the next reader can see what they do.

rules.name: no-destructive-sql
rules.reason: DROP TABLE against a live database is unrecoverable without a restore, and the argument arrived quoted so nothing textual would have caught it. Write the change as a reversible migration and run it through the project's migration harness.

rules.name: no-git-add-all-anywhere
rules.reason: `git add -A` sweeps in unintended files (secrets, temp files, generated artifacts), and wrapping it in `bash -lc` or a subshell does not change that. Stage paths explicitly with `git add <path> ...`, or `git add -u` for tracked-only changes.

rules.name: watch-opaque-commands
rules.reason: Observational only — this call is NOT blocked. The command text does not say what it will run: the command word is a variable nothing in the text assigns, or the program arrives through `eval` or a decoder. Recorded so the operator can see how often that shape occurs before deciding whether it warrants a prompt.

rules.name: echoing-a-command-name-is-fine
rules.reason: Pre-approved: naming a command inside an `echo` is documentation, not execution, and this rule exists so the structural matchers have something to prove they are structural.

tests.command: bash -lc 'cd /repo && git add -A && git commit -m wip'
